bib.title: The No-U-Turn Sampler: Adaptively Setting Path Lengths in Hamiltonian Monte Carlo

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "The No-U-Turn Sampler: Adaptively Setting Path Lengths in Hamiltonian Monte Carlo", Matthew D. Hoffman and Andrew Gelman. The PDF stamp reads "arXiv:1111.4246v1 [stat.CO] 18 Nov 2011". It is an arXiv preprint. The running header says "Hoffman and Gelman" and "The No-U-Turn Sampler". There is no journal name in the extracted text. The paper was later published in JMLR in 2014, but that is not printed in this PDF, so do not cite it from this source.

COVERAGE: Whole file read. 30 pages, 78,364 chars, including the derivation, Algorithms 1-6, experiments, discussion, Appendix A and references (skimmed). I did not read the detailed proofs of the simplified Algorithm 2 (about sections 3.1.1, equations 6-9) line by line. Figure plots are axis text only. No scan or garble problems.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- NUTS removes the need to hand-set the number of leapfrog steps L, and with dual averaging it needs no hand-tuning.
  number: none
  setup: extension of HMC; step size adapted during burn-in, then frozen.
  quote: "We introduce the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS), an extension to HMC that eliminates the need to set a number of steps L."
  where: abstract, p1
- Mechanism: NUTS doubles a trajectory (1, 2, 4, ... steps) in a random direction. It stops when the subtrajectory from the leftmost to the rightmost leaf of any balanced subtree starts to double back.
  number: none
  setup: slice variable u, balanced binary tree, U-turn test (θ+−θ−)·r ≥ 0 at both ends (Algorithm 3).
  quote: "The doubling is halted when the subtrajectory from the leftmost to the rightmost nodes of any balanced subtree of the overall binary tree starts to double back on itself (i.e., the ﬁctional particle starts to make a “U-turn”)."
  where: p7
- The naive stop rule (stop when the dot product goes below 0) is not time-reversible. The tree doubling is what restores correct sampling.
  number: none
  setup: derivative of half the squared distance from the start, (θ̃−θ)·r̃.
  quote: "Unfortunately this algorithm does not guarantee time reversibility, and is therefore not guaranteed to converge to the correct distribution."
  where: p5
- Efficiency, NUTS vs HMC: NUTS matches HMC on the two logistic regressions and beats HMC's best ESS by about 3x on the multivariate normal and stochastic volatility problems.
  number: about 3x
  setup: metric is ESS per gradient evaluation. Compared against the best of 10 HMC simulation lengths. 2000 iterations, first 1000 used for burn-in and adaptation. 10 seeds per setting. Four targets: 250-D MVN; logistic regression on German credit (25 parameters); hierarchical logistic regression (301 parameters); stochastic volatility (3001 parameters, 3000 S&P 500 days).
  quote: "On the multivariate normal and stochastic volatility problems, NUTS with δ = 0.6 outperforms HMC’s best ESS by about a factor of three."
  where: p25
- HMC's best simulation length varies about 100x across problems, so HMC needs preliminary tuning runs.
  number: about 100x (optimal λ from 0.17 to 17.62)
  setup: same four targets.
  quote: "the best simulation lengths λ for HMC varied by about a factor of 100, with the longest optimal λ being 17.62 (for the multivari-ate normal) and the shortest optimal λ being 0.17 (for the simple logistic regression)."
  where: p25
- Recommended target acceptance rate: δ = 0.65 for HMC and δ = 0.6 for NUTS. NUTS performance is flat for δ in [0.45, 0.65]. The paper's own defaults use δ = 0.65 in Fig 4 and 0.5 in the Fig 7 demo. This is later superseded in practice; Stan and PyMC default to 0.8 (my knowledge, not in the paper).
  number: 0.65 / 0.6
  setup: δ swept over 0.25-0.95 (15 values for NUTS, 8 for HMC).
  quote: "HMC’s best performance seems to occur around δ = 0.65, suggesting that this is indeed a reasonable default value for a variety of problems. NUTS’s best performance seems to occur around δ = 0.6, but does not seem to depend strongly on δ within the range δ∈ [0.45, 0.65]."
  where: p25
- Step-size adaptation uses Nesterov dual averaging. The same hyperparameters were used in all experiments, and the authors concede they were hand-picked on one model.
  number: γ=0.05, t0=10, κ=0.75
  setup: tuned by hand on the stochastic volatility model. Adaptation runs for M_adapt burn-in iterations, then ε is fixed to the averaged iterate ε̄.
  quote: "We used the values γ = 0.05,t 0 = 10, and κ = 0.75 for all our experiments."
  where: p16
- Initial step-size heuristic (Algorithm 4): double or halve ε until the Langevin proposal's acceptance probability crosses 0.5. The shrinkage target is μ = log(10ε1), which biases the search toward larger ε because larger ε is cheaper.
  number: 0.5; factor 10
  setup: Algorithms 4-6.
  quote: "We recommend settingµ = log(10ϵ1), since this gives the dual averaging algorithm a preference for testing values of ϵ that are larger than the initial value ϵ1."
  where: p19
- NUTS's acceptance statistic is an average over all states in the final doubling: H_t = (1/|B_final|) Σ min{1, p(θ,r)/p(θ_{t-1},r_{t,0})}. There is no single accept/reject step in NUTS.
  number: none
  setup: eq. 19; Algorithm 6 implements it as α/n_α.
  quote: "HNUTS can be understood as the average acceptance probability that HMC would give to the position-momentum states explored during the ﬁnal doubling iteration."
  where: p17
- Dual averaging convergence: ε̄ roughly converges within a few hundred iterations, except for stochastic volatility, which needs a longer burn-in. The realized acceptance statistic is closest to δ on the other models and worse on SV (Fig 3).
  number: "a few hundred" iterations
  setup: NUTS, δ = 0.65, four models.
  quote: "Except for the stochastic volatility model, which requires longer to burn in, ¯ϵ roughly converges within a few hundred iterations."
  where: p22
- Trajectory lengths are mostly powers of two, so the U-turn is usually triggered at the end of a doubling and not by an inner subtree. Trajectory length grows as δ grows, because the step size ε gets smaller.
  number: none
  setup: Fig 5 histograms over δ = 0.25..0.95, four models.
  quote: "Most of the tra-jectory lengths are integer powers of two"
  where: p23
- Visual comparison on the 250-D correlated normal: RWM and Gibbs barely explore the space after 1,000,000 iterations. NUTS gets many effectively independent samples from about 1,000,000 gradient evaluations.
  number: 1,000,000 RWM iterations / Gibbs sweeps vs 2,000 NUTS iterations
  setup: NUTS δ=0.5, 1000 burn-in. RWM proposal variance set for 0.234 acceptance. Informal, plotted on the first two dimensions only.
  quote: "RWM has barely begun to explore the space. Gibbs does better, but still has left parts of the space unexplored."
  where: p26
- Scaling with dimension D: HMC costs about O(D^{5/4}) per independent sample. RWM costs O(D^2). Gibbs also needs O(D^2) even under optimistic assumptions.
  number: O(D^{5/4}) vs O(D^2)
  setup: cited from Creutz 1988 for the HMC and RWM costs. This is theory, not measured in this paper.
  quote: "The cost of HMC per indepen-dent sample from a target distribution of dimension D is roughly O(D5/4), which stands in sharp contrast with the O(D2) cost of random-walk Metropolis (Creutz, 1988)."
  where: p2
- ESS estimator (Appendix A): truncate the autocorrelation sum where it first drops below 0.05. Mean and variance come from a separate 50,000-iteration NUTS run (δ=0.5), not from the chain being measured. The authors say it gave more reliable confidence intervals than the CODA autoregressive approach. Reported ESS is the minimum over dimensions, computed from both the mean and the second moment.
  number: 0.05 cutoff; 50,000 iterations
  setup: the cutoff is "somewhat arbitrary".
  quote: "we truncate the sum over the autocorrelations when the autocorrelations ﬁrst dip below 0.05"
  where: p28-29
- Handling constraints and discrete variables. NUTS and HMC work only on unconstrained continuous variables that are differentiable almost everywhere. Constraints need a change of variable. Discrete variables must be summed out or handled by Gibbs. At a zero-probability region, HMC wastes its whole trajectory, while NUTS stops short and samples from the points visited so far.
  number: none
  setup: discussion.
  quote: "Like HMC, NUTS can only be used to resample unconstrained continuous-valued vari-ables with respect to which the target distribution is diﬀerentiable almost everywhere."
  where: p27
- Memory: the simple version stores 2^j states. The efficient version (Algorithm 3) stores O(j) states, using a delayed-rejection-like kernel that favors the new half-tree with probability min{1, n′/n}. The cost is about 2^j − 1 gradient evaluations per iteration.
  number: O(j) vs 2^j
  setup: sections 3.1.2, Algorithms 2-3.
  quote: "This kernel admits a memory-eﬃcient implementation that only requires that we store O(j) position and momentum vectors, rather than O(2j)."
  where: p12
- Motivation for the PyMC/Stan connection. The paper names PyMC (Patil et al., 2010) among the generic engines that HMC could not be put into because of the L parameter. It says NUTS is the core of the planned Stan, which "promises" to generate effectively independent samples "orders of magnitude faster than previous systems such as BUGS and JAGS". This is a promise, not a measured result.
  number: none
  quote: "Stan promises to be able to generate eﬀectively independent samples from complex models’ posteriors orders of magnitude faster than previous systems such as BUGS and JAGS."
  where: p27-28

LIMITS
- NUTS is compared only against basic HMC. The authors say: "we have only compared NUTS with the basic HMC algorithm, and not its extensions".
- Only the identity mass matrix (kinetic energy ½ r·r) was used. A mass matrix approximating the covariance is named as a possible benefit for both NUTS and HMC but is not tested. Adapting the mass matrix is not in this paper.
- The dual averaging hyperparameters were hand-chosen on the SV model. The authors say they "may not work as well for other sampling algorithms or for H statistics other than the ones described".
- Dual averaging adapts less well on the SV model, which has the longest burn-in. This is worst for HMC with small δ.
- Only four targets, all with a smooth unimodal-ish posterior. No divergence diagnostics and no multimodality or funnel (hierarchical geometry) analysis. The "Δmax" divergence check appears in the pseudocode only as a stop criterion. I did not find its numeric value in the text I read. Stan's divergence concept is not discussed.
- The authors suggest part of the gain over HMC may come from NUTS having no single accept/reject step, and not only from path length. This is a hypothesis, not tested.
- Cost is measured in gradient evaluations, not wall-clock time.
- Dated: Matlab code, with C++ promised in Stan. Later practice (default δ, mass-matrix adaptation, multinomial sampling) is not covered here.

CODE
Leapfrog (Algorithm 1, p3):
  Set r̃←r + (ε/2)∇θL(θ).
  Set θ̃←θ + εr̃.
  Set r̃←r̃ + (ε/2)∇θL(θ̃).
Stop rule (Algorithm 3, p14): "s←s′I[(θ+−θ−)·r−≥ 0]I[(θ+−θ−)·r+≥ 0]"
Dual averaging update (Algorithm 6, p18): "Set ¯Hm = (1 − 1/(m+t0)) ¯Hm−1 + 1/(m+t0) (δ−α/nα)". Then "Set logϵm = µ − (√m/γ) ¯Hm, log ¯ϵm = m^{−κ} logϵm + (1−m^{−κ}) log ¯ϵm−1." After M_adapt, "Set ϵm = ¯ϵM adapt."
Initial ε heuristic (Algorithm 4, p17): "Initialize ϵ = 1 ... a← 2I[p(θ′,r′)/p(θ,r) > 0.5] − 1. while (p(θ′,r′)/p(θ,r))^a > 2^{−a} do ϵ← 2^a ϵ."

FIGURES (the captions tool was not run; these are from the extracted text)
- Fig 1, p5: building a binary tree by repeated doubling, with forward and backward directions chosen at random. Best visual of the algorithm.
- Fig 2, p6: one NUTS iteration. The U-turn is shown as the angle between the blue and magenta arrows being more than 90 degrees. Nodes excluded for the slice or for detailed balance are shown as red markers.
- Fig 3, p21: realized vs target acceptance statistic (dual averaging works).
- Fig 4, p22: ε̄ convergence within a few hundred iterations at δ = 0.65.
- Fig 5, p23: trajectory-length histograms are powers of 2.
- Fig 6, p24: ESS per gradient vs δ and ε·L. This is the main result figure.
- Fig 7, p25: 250-D normal, NUTS vs RWM vs Gibbs. Visually the clearest for the note.

PROBLEMS
- Math symbols and subscripts are garbled by extraction (for example "O(D5/4)" and "2 j" for 2^j). Quotes are verbatim from the extraction, so exponents appear flattened.
- Ligatures such as "ﬁ" and "ﬀ" appear in the quotes.
- No embedded instructions found.
- I did not confirm the Δmax value or the exact wording of the BuildTree docs in the unread proof sections.
